title: The St. Louis season, meeting his first wife Alma, and being let go in Memphis
summary: He plays the New Orleans and St. Louis seasons, Captain Joe coaches him to sing, he meets Alma, and is told 'the axe is on you' as Red returns, with a bonus and pay from the Streckfus company.

story.theme_name: Dance halls, lake camps and riverboat bandstands
story.community_name: Working the Streckfus riverboats with Fate Marable

blocks.x: Well, Eckerhardt, Lewis Eckerhardt, that's what it was, yeah. He seemingly was a fellow just out of, youngster just out of school and everything, but he was a very good musician, he could read anything, but his lips didn't allow him to go too high, and they kept him on second, you see, and they tried a couple of times to put him on lead, but he just didn't have the punch to play a solo, or even take a hot solo, you see. At that particular time, but he eventually learned later on. So as I say, I worked on a boat that particular year, I played that season here, and I went to St. Louis, and I played the fourth season, but during that season in St. Louis, they were still dicking on time to get a fellow, but they had before me, before Willie Foster, what was his name? He was a little short, but he looked like a white man to me. He used to be with the Cab Calloway band when he was on Chicago, his name would come to me. He was a very eccentric banjo player. He was a novelty man, he could sing, he could entertain, because I remember there was one song out that had what they call a parody to it, he was very good on, Laugh Clown Laugh, I remember that well. Well at that time I didn't do nothing but play, I didn't sing, I even couldn't talk a song or nothing, so there was a Captain John on the boat, he used to always tell me, he said, why don't you try to do some little thing besides just playing, you see. He said, you know Red was a, that was his name was Red, that's what it was. He said Red was a, well he was a clown in the world, he could do everything, you see, put the banjo around his neck and everything, you see, and that's what people like, you see, and even sing. So Captain Joe used to come down and rehearse a band sometimes in St. Louis, and he, I remember one time he started me to sing a number, I mean his name of the song was about, sing something about Hallelujah in it, and another song he had me used to get up there, he even showed me how to do it, well, that went over pretty good, you see. Well all this, the whole time St. Louis they was trying to get Red, but they couldn't get him, you see, so that's where I met my, the first woman I married, my first wife named Alma, you see, and I eventually played the season in St. Louis, so on the way coming back to New Orleans, I got the word that Red was going to meet the boat in Memphis, and that's where I would be discharged, you see. So at that time they always had the word on the boat when you're going to know it's going to get fired, they used to have the sail, well the axe is going to drop on sail, they call it the axe. The axe was the boat, you know, the carriage that actually used for the, you know, like that person having a fire, you know, and those things, and they say, well man, the axe is on you now. And Faith used to have a piano song about don't talk about me when I'm gone, and everybody said, well, no, somebody leaving. Well, the only thing I didn't take it so hard, because I had the opportunity to see many guys go when I was there, you know. So they were very good to me, the Stratford Company, they had let me go a week before my time, I mean a couple days before my time, and they paid me for that week, and they gave me, they always give you a bonus, you know, like when you make that particular season, I got that back, and I stayed on Memphis about a week or so.
Well, to interrupt you again, would the Stratford Spiders musicians or anything? Oh yes, yes.
